Breti Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Breti, Georgia

Demolished. Breti, on the Prone River near Kareli, has deep Christian roots tied to Father Pyrrhus, one of the Thirteen Assyrian Fathers who strengthened Georgian Christianity in the 6th century. Jewish settlement history is disputed among scholars - one source suggests centuries-long presence, another traces migration from southern Georgia via Vakhani in the 16th century. The Avalishvili noble family settled in Breti in 1605 with their Jewish serfs; further Jewish migration occurred from Akhaldaba, Akhaltsikhe, and Vakhani in the 1680s, and from Tamarasheni in 1749. Only 25 Jewish families remained by 1870, most relocating that year to Tskhinvali, Kareli, or Surami. Breti is also famous for the 'Bible of Breti' - a parchment manuscript handwritten in 1513, owned by the Avalishvili family since the 17th century, believed by both Jews and Georgians to hold miraculous healing powers. This cemetery was active until the early 20th century; exact dates can no longer be determined since no tombstones remain on site. Since 2008 the land has been privately owned and converted to farmland; its tombstones were cleared and dumped in the local river that same year.
